title: Waterspout Behind Your Boat in the Dark. Now What?
logline: Alone at night south of Bermuda, an exhausted sailor misses the waterspout forming behind him. Once he sees it, running fails, and NOAA's ninety-degree rule is what gets him clear before the squall hits.
essence: Alone at night, you beat a waterspout not by running, but by turning ninety degrees to its path.

hero.name: Kai (you)
hero.description: Solo sailor in his thirties on a 32-ft sloop. Yellow foul-weather jacket, red headlamp, salt-stiff hair. The narrator addresses him as 'you'.
hero.flaw: Exhausted after a long single-handed watch, with no crew and an unreliable engine. He watches the bow and forgets to look behind.

hook.visual: Frame 0: Kai at the tiller, headlamp-lit face strained and wide-eyed, staring at the compass. Behind his starboard quarter a moonlit spray ring is already spinning. The camera is mid dolly-in. Warm face against deep blue-teal sea.

core_question.text: How do you survive a waterspout spinning up beside your boat at night?

stakes.physical: Vortex winds and flying spray can knock the boat down and throw you across the cockpit.
stakes.legal_ethical: Alone at sea, every call is yours. No crew covers a lapse, and help is only a channel-sixteen call away.
stakes.mortal: Thrown overboard at night without a tether, you drown alone.

ticking_clock.what: SQUALL ETA badge counting down to the squall line that spawned the spout

spine.once_upon_a_time: A tired solo sailor crossed the dark water south of Bermuda.
spine.every_day: You stand the night watch alone, eyes on the compass, trusting the boat.
spine.one_day: A waterspout spins up behind your stern while a squall line builds ahead.
because_of_that: Because of that, you race the squall by reaching for the engine. It dies, and only then do you turn and see the spout.
Because of that, you run straight downwind, but your lead won't grow while the spout matures into a full vortex.
Because of that, you clip in, read its track, and throw the tiller over ninety degrees to its motion.
spine.until_finally: Until finally the vortex tears past your stern and decays, and the squall breaks over a tethered, reefed boat.
spine.ever_since: Ever since then, you look back before you look ahead.

beats.name: HOOK
beats.summary: The spray ring spins behind Kai's stern. He is staring at the compass and has not seen it.

beats.name: CONTEXT
beats.summary: He is alone inside the Triangle with no crew. Lightning flickers in the squall line ahead while he works the chartplotter. Thunder makes him look up, and the squall clock starts.

beats.name: ESCALATION_1
beats.summary: He reaches for the engine to beat the squall, and it dies. A hiss turns him around: stage three, spray ring. He runs straight downwind, but his lead won't grow.

beats.name: MIDPOINT
beats.summary: Lightning reveals a mature vortex from sea to cloud, towering over the sloop. Some waterspouts are tornadoes over water.

beats.name: ESCALATION_2
beats.summary: Step one: life jacket and tether. Step two: read its track. Close-up decision, then step three: turn ninety degrees to its motion. It roars past the stern and decays.

beats.name: PAYOFF
beats.summary: The squall still slams in, and he rides it on his tether. The catch: NOAA finds no extra disappearances in the Triangle. Weather kills, and ninety degrees beats it.

beats.name: STING
beats.summary: Rain lifts, and Kai glances back over his shoulder. A hard stop loops into frame 0.

narration.text: A dark waterspout is twisting behind your boat.
narration.adds: Names the thing and says it is behind you, outside the hero's view.

narration.text: You're alone, south of Bermuda, inside the famous Triangle.
narration.adds: Places the empty sea on the map and loads it with the Triangle legend.

narration.text: No crew to wake. Only you and channel sixteen.
narration.adds: States the rules: no backup, and the radio is the only lifeline.

narration.text: But the squall comes first, so you reach for the engine.
narration.adds: Gives the motive: he is racing the squall, still blind to the spout.

narration.text: That spray ring is stage three of five.
narration.adds: Turns a splash into a stage on a known life cycle, with two stages still to come.

narration.text: Your instinct says run. Straight downwind, away from it.
narration.adds: Voices the hero's gut choice before we see him act on it.
Reads the outcome of the run: the distance is not opening.

narration.text: Then stage four arrives: a mature vortex, sea to cloud.
narration.adds: Names the stage, so the towering image reads as escalation, not spectacle.

narration.text: Worse: some are simply tornadoes over open water.
narration.adds: The #2 fact: this can carry tornado strength, which the picture cannot prove.

narration.text: Step one: your life jacket on, tether clipped. Because three in four boating deaths are drownings.
narration.adds: Explains why the jacket matters, with the Coast Guard drowning statistic.

narration.text: Then step two: read its track, because your escape depends on its direction.
narration.adds: Explains the purpose of watching it: direction, not distance, decides the escape.

narration.text: Step three: turn your bow ninety degrees to its motion. Because sideways clears its path.
narration.adds: Gives the counter-intuitive rule and its reason: step sideways instead of fleeing.

narration.text: Then stage five: decay. You're clear.
narration.adds: Names the final stage, so the fraying funnel reads as over rather than regrouping.

narration.text: Here's the catch: NOAA finds no extra disappearances in the Triangle.
narration.adds: The #1 surprise: the legend was never the threat.

narration.text: Weather kills. You beat it at ninety degrees, never closer.
narration.adds: Answers the core question in one rule you can remember.

narration.text: Out here, you always look back, because
narration.adds: An unfinished sentence that the first line completes on replay.

steps.instruction: Life jacket on, tether clipped to the jackline.
steps.because: Three in four boating deaths are drownings.

steps.instruction: Read the waterspout's track, its apparent direction of motion.
steps.because: The escape heading depends on its direction.

steps.instruction: Turn ninety degrees to its motion, never closer.
steps.because: Sideways takes you out of its path; NOAA advises a 90-degree move away and never approaching.

facts.claim: NOAA advises boaters encountering a waterspout to move away at a 90-degree angle to its apparent movement and never to move closer to investigate.
facts.source_title: What is a waterspout? (NOAA National Ocean Service)

facts.claim: Tornadic waterspouts are tornadoes that form over water or move from land to water, with the same characteristics as land tornadoes.
facts.source_title: What is a waterspout? (NOAA National Ocean Service)

facts.claim: Waterspouts develop through five stages: dark spot, spiral pattern, spray ring, mature vortex, and decay.
In U.S. Coast Guard recreational boating statistics, where cause of death was known, about 75% of fatal boating accident victims drowned.
facts.source_title: Accident Statistics (U.S. Coast Guard Boating Safety)

facts.claim: Marine VHF channel 16 is the international distress, safety and calling channel.

NOAA says there is no evidence that mysterious disappearances occur more often in the Bermuda Triangle than in any other large, well-traveled area of ocean; environmental factors explain most, if not all, of them.
facts.source_title: Is there such a thing as the Bermuda Triangle? (NOAA National Ocean Service)

suspense_devices.desc: The spray ring spins behind Kai from frame 0 (S01-S02). He notices it only at 14.6 s.
The audience knows about the spout, and then the squall lightning, while Kai works the chartplotter and the engine.
The life jacket and tether hang on the companionway hook in S04 (6 s). They are clipped on in step one (32 s) and hold him through the squall.
Lightning reveals the full mature vortex from sea to cloud.
Core question: how do you survive it? Closed by L15.

attempts.action: Start the engine to motor clear of the squall
Run straight downwind, away from the spout
Life jacket on, tether clipped to the jackline
Read the spout's track against the shroud
Tiller hard over, turning ninety degrees to its motion

resolution.hero_action: Kai clips in, reads the spout's track and turns ninety degrees to its motion instead of fleeing downwind.
resolution.outcome: The vortex passes astern and decays. The squall hits a tethered, reefed boat, and Kai rides it out soaked, with a torn jib.

loop_back.desc: L16 'Out here, you always look back, because' is completed on replay by L01 'A dark waterspout is twisting behind your boat.'

open_loops.desc: Core question: how do you survive a waterspout at night?
Will the engine start in time?
Stage three of five: what are the next stages?
Will running downwind open the gap?
Which way do you turn once you've read its track?
Squall at 03:00: will you be ready when it hits?

overrides.reason: The ninety-degree method is taught as step three in ESCALATION_2, because the hero must act on it at the threat's peak. L15 in the payoff restates it as the CQ answer alongside the #1 surprise fact, so the gap closes formally within 0.80-0.95D.

narrator.persona: Calm-under-pressure delivery skipper talking you through your own night, energetic but never shouty
narrator.authority: Speaks only NOAA and U.S. Coast Guard guidance and statistics; every number is sourced
narrator.direction: Tight and urgent in the hook and steps, dropping to near-whisper on L03, L09 and L16. Slower and weighted through the payoff. Silence in every gap; never talk over the close-ups.

threats.desc: A waterspout forms off the starboard quarter, behind the hero, and matures into a vortex.
The squall line with lightning ahead, bringing a violent gust and rain.

knowledge_timeline.audience_question: Who could even help you out here?
Will the engine start before you see the spout?
What beats a tornado on water?
Will the turn come in time?
Was the Triangle ever the real danger?

Breath; lightning flickers unseen behind Kai.
